bug_semantics: A deserialization gadget carrier that performs JavaBeans property reads, most notably a collection sorted by Apache Commons BeanUtils BeanComparator, can treat the no-argument JDBC methods getConnection() and getPooledConnection() as readable properties named connection and pooledConnection. If an attacker-controlled serialized c3p0 DataSource or ConnectionPoolDataSource is configured to reach a susceptible JDBC driver, the property read invokes that driver-facing method during deserialization and can trigger the driver's dangerous behavior.
flaw_origin: c3p0 made its JDBC DataSource implementations Serializable and deliberately JavaBean-style while exposing public no-argument getConnection()/getPooledConnection() methods, but shipped no explicit BeanInfo that excluded those resource-producing methods from introspection. The vulnerable combination is already present in c3p0's first public 0.8 release, before the repository's reconstructed Git history begins, so the development commit that originated it is not publicly represented.
ai_marker: not assessable: no real BIC commit object exists in the accessible history. The earliest boundary object, 66e3716e788e0ac8f9c2e8e93711cfee301bede8, has Steve Waldman as author and committer and no trailers or bot identity, but it is a reconstructed SourceForge release-snapshot import rather than the commit that authored the vulnerable mechanism, so its absent AI marker cannot be used to attribute the BIC.
evidence: The first-party GHSA states that versions < 0.14.0 are affected and 0.14.0 is the first patched version. It explains that malicious DataSource/ConnectionPoolDataSource objects can be placed in deserialization contexts that automatically read JavaBean properties, causing getConnection()/getPooledConnection() to enter susceptible JDBC drivers; https://github.com/swaldman/c3p0/security/advisories/GHSA-w6w4-rjh9-9r58.

git grep at the earliest nonempty reconstructed-history commit 66e3716e788e0ac8f9c2e8e93711cfee301bede8 finds the dangerous no-argument methods at src/classes/com/mchange/v2/c3p0/DriverManagerDataSource.java:61, JndiRefDataSource.java:102, PoolBackedDataSource.java:56, and WrapperConnectionPoolDataSource.java:72. The same snapshot's BeangenDataSourceGenerator.java:66 adds IndirectingSerializableExtension to generated DataSource bases, and DriverManagerDataSourceFactory.java documents that returned DataSources are Referenceable and Serializable.

git cat-file commit 66e3716e788e0ac8f9c2e8e93711cfee301bede8 identifies it as 'source imported from SourceForge (c3p0-0.8.4-test1.src.zip)' with parent 0457a1a6340cff65ee20927c36646bf55e95ba83. git rev-list -n 1 c3p0-0.8.4-test1 resolves the tag to that import. This is a whole-release snapshot reconstruction, not a development BIC and not decomposable into member commits in the validated clone.

Direct parent-tree verification with git ls-tree -r --name-only 0457a1a6340cff65ee20927c36646bf55e95ba83 returns no paths: the parent is the explicitly empty reconstruction root. That proves only that the vulnerable sources enter this Git reconstruction at the snapshot boundary; it does not prove that the snapshot import authored them.

SourceForge's first-party historical downloads page publishes c3p0-0.8 from 2001-04-17 and its README calls 0.8 the first public release, explicitly describing 'Referenceable and Serializable implementations of DataSources' and saying the DataSources are written in JavaBean style. This predates the clone's earliest source snapshot, c3p0-0.8.4-test1 from 2003, and proves the vulnerable design existed before 66e3716e788e0ac8f9c2e8e93711cfee301bede8; https://sourceforge.net/projects/c3p0/files/historical/OldFiles/.

The validated clone has no c3p0-0.8 or c3p0-0.8.1 development ancestry: git tag --list 'c3p0-0.8*' begins at c3p0-0.8.4-test1. Its other root, 7ff5d91ae823c8fb9dcdd3f040d274a94bcf4aa6, is itself labeled 'Initial commit after migration to git' in 2012 and bulk-adds the already mature source, so it is also not a BIC.

The advisory-linked direct fix 7b022c4b6694dabc6204254dc917af9c38f2cb27 adds beanInfo/src/com/mchange/v2/c3p0/beaninfo/C3P0BeanInfoGen.java and build.mill generation/packaging. The generator excludes property names connection and pooledConnection and property types java.sql.Connection and javax.sql.PooledConnection. Its parent is e604f8d7599e185803a7fa6584f7076331cbc847, whose tree has no beanInfo path.

The immediate follow-up 18eca22d96048c087c624bc5f46b6ac8d6d4d699 adds PerishableConnectionResourcesNotBeanPropertiesJUnitTestCase, documenting and checking that Introspector exposes neither forbidden property names nor resource types for the shipped DataSource classes. This corroborates the fix mechanism; the advisory correctly links the implementation commit 7b022c4b6694dabc6204254dc917af9c38f2cb27 as the direct fix.

Version-boundary checks resolve v0.13.0 to a8f08227431ebc00bb75486011675b103cff1643 and show its tree has the vulnerable DataSource implementations but no beanInfo source. git tag --contains 7b022c4b6694dabc6204254dc917af9c38f2cb27 returns only v0.14.0 and v0.14.1; v0.14.0 resolves to 931fd53b695720adc4ac087e021b6de7daf0dd1b and contains C3P0BeanInfoGen.java. Thus the fix lands exactly at the declared 0.14.0 patched boundary.
reasoning: The security defect is not that JDBC DataSource has a method named getConnection() by itself; it is the composition of c3p0's serializable, JavaBean-style DataSource objects, dangerous no-argument resource getters, and the absence of explicit BeanInfo suppressing those pseudo-properties. A deserialization carrier can therefore perform what appears to be a property read but actually opens a JDBC connection and executes driver code. Commit 7b022c4b6694dabc6204254dc917af9c38f2cb27 closes that route by generating and packaging explicit BeanInfo for all relevant implementations, excluding the methods by both property name and return type, and it is present starting in v0.14.0. For origin, git -S/grep/history inspection reaches 66e3716e788e0ac8f9c2e8e93711cfee301bede8, whose empty immediate parent lacks every vulnerable line. However, the commit message and tag prove that object is a reconstructed import of the complete 0.8.4-test1 source release, while the first-party 0.8 release archive documents the same serializable JavaBean DataSource design two years earlier. Treating the import or the separate 2012 Git migration root as the BIC would violate the protocol's ban on release/squash aggregates. Because the pre-0.8 development history needed to identify the smallest commit is absent, there is no genuine BIC commit object on which to make an AI-only judgment; this is a genuine public-history boundary and therefore BLOCKED rather than NOT_AI or EVIDENCE_GAP.
remaining_gap: The missing fact is the smallest pre-April-2001 development commit that first combined a serializable c3p0 DataSource/ConnectionPoolDataSource with introspectable getConnection()/getPooledConnection() and no excluding BeanInfo, together with that commit's immediate parent and commit object. The validated repository begins with later whole-source imports, and the available first-release archive is a snapshot rather than commit history, so this origin and its AI marker cannot be recovered from public history.
